decisions.quote: Eyal, Liberman, and Trope (2008) established that people judged moral transgressions more harshly and virtuous acts more positively when the acts were psychologically distant than close. In a series of conceptual and direct replications, Gong and Medin (2012) came to the opposite conclusion. Attempting to resolve these inconsistencies, we conducted four high-powered replication studies in which we varied temporal distance (Studies 1 and 3), social distance (Study 2) or construal level (Study 4), and registered their impact on moral judgment. We found no systematic effect of temporal distance, the effect of social distance consistent with Eyal et al., and the reversed effect of direct construal level manipulation, consistent with Gong and Medin.
decisions.reason: The primary source text (`fe0e494e6758464b.txt`) consists solely of the title and abstract of Żurawski (2014; DOI `10.1027/1864-9335/a000188`) and does not include the full text or reference list. The abstract states that the authors conducted four high-powered replication studies varying temporal distance (Studies 1 and 3), social distance (Study 2), or construal level (Study 4) to resolve inconsistencies between Eyal, Liberman, and Trope (2008; shipped row 165, DOI `10.1016/j.jesp.2008.03.012`, coded as sibling target 0) and Gong and Medin (2012), and reports that the reversed effect of direct construal level manipulation was consistent with Gong and Medin. However, the abstract provides only the in-text author-year citation 'Gong and Medin (2012)' without a bibliography entry, work title, or DOI. Because confirming a `blind_right` missing row requires a complete source-backed original identity (including a nonempty `title`) and missing bibliographic identifiers cannot be invented from outside the primary source, the full bibliographic identity of the Gong and Medin (2012) work and which specific studies or findings from it were empirically re-tested remain unresolved from the abstract-only source.

decisions.quote: Recent work has found an affective priming effect using the naming task: In pronouncing target words, pronunciation latencies were consistently shorter when the target (e.g., loyal) was preceded by an evaluatively congruent (e.g., sunshine) rather than incongruent prime word (e.g, rain). Using the naming task, no affective priming was found in the present studies irrespective of prime-set size and target-set size (Experiment 1), irrespective of stimulus-onset asynchrony (Experiment 2), and even when a nearly exact replication of previous work that demonstrated the effect was conducted (Experiment 3).
decisions.reason: The primary source (`fed9b2985183e3e8.txt`) contains only the title and abstract of Klauer and Musch (2001; DOI `10.1080/713755986`). The abstract states that Experiment 3 was 'a nearly exact replication of previous work that demonstrated the effect' (an affective priming effect using the naming/pronunciation task), and that no affective priming was found, but the abstract gives no citation, author names, year, or title for that previous work. The single shipped row (row 1010: Bargh, Chaiken, Raymond, & Hymes, 1996, 'The Automatic Evaluation Effect: Unconditional Automatic Attitude Activation with a Pronunciation Task', DOI `10.1006/jesp.1996.0005`) is a known paper demonstrating automatic evaluation with a pronunciation task, and the blind coder recorded only a single unnamed target for Experiment 3. Because the abstract-only source text does not name or cite the original work replicated in Experiment 3, it is undeterminable from the available primary evidence whether Experiment 3 re-tests the already-shipped Bargh et al. (1996) paper in row 1010 or a different original work.

decisions.quote: This is a replication study of ASR and the first study of P50 suppression in Russian patients with schizophrenia (n = 28) and healthy controls (n = 25). ASR and P50 were estimated according to standard protocols. Patients exhibited increased baseline ASR latency (d = 0.35, p = .026) and reduced prepulse inhibition (PPI) at 60 ms interval (d = 0.39, p = .003) and 120 ms interval (d = 0.37, p = .005) relative to controls.
decisions.reason: The primary source (`fefb1a617468c079.txt`) contains only the title and abstract of Kirenskaya et al. (2016; DOI `10.1017/sjp.2016.1`). The abstract states that 'This is a replication study of ASR and the first study of P50 suppression in Russian patients with schizophrenia (n = 28) and healthy controls (n = 25),' and reports increased baseline ASR latency and reduced prepulse inhibition (PPI) at 60 ms and 120 ms intervals in patients relative to controls, but does not name or cite the original acoustic startle response (ASR) study being replicated. The single shipped row (row 720: Storozheva, Kirenskaya, Lazarev, Novototskii-Vlasov, Samylkin, & Fastovtsov, 2011, 'Prepulse Modification of the Acoustic Startle Reaction in Healthy Subjects and Patients with Schizophrenia', DOI `10.1007/s11055-011-9545-z`) is an earlier ASR/PPI study in schizophrenia patients and healthy controls by overlapping authors, and the blind coder recorded only this single unnamed target. Because the abstract-only source text does not identify the original work, the unresolved question is whether the unnamed ASR replication target in the abstract is the shipped Storozheva et al. (2011) paper (row 720) or a distinct original study.

corrected_value.authors: Nosek, B. A., & Smyth, F. L.
corrected_value.title: Implicit social cognitions predict sex differences in math engagement and achievement.

decisions.quote:
Nosek and Smyth (2011) compared the gender-science IAT and the explicit

stereotype (measured with two self-reported items: Men are better at math than women are

and Women can achieve as much as men in math) in predicting math-related outcomes. We

re-analyzed that data and found only one variable, the difference between math and verbal

SAT scores, that had reliably stronger relation with the IAT (r = .193, p < .001) than the

explicit stereotype (r = .090, p = .004), Williams' t(1040) = 2.590, p = .010.
decisions.reason: In Part 2 of the full text (pp. 13–14, lines 387–441; Discussion p. 18, lines 536–547), the authors explicitly re-analyze the original dataset of Nosek and Smyth (2011; full citation in References p. 27, lines 803–806: Nosek, B. A., & Smyth, F. L. (2011). Implicit social cognitions predict sex differences in math engagement and achievement. American Educational Research Journal, 48(5), 1125-1156. doi: 10.3102/0002831211410683) to test whether the gender-science IAT's advantage over explicit stereotypes in predicting math-related outcomes (specifically the math-minus-verbal SAT difference score, r = .193 vs. r = .090, Williams' t(1040) = 2.590, p = .010) persists when controlling for self-reported math attitudes (finding the partial correlations r = .049 vs. r = .017 no longer significantly differ, Williams' t(1040) < 1, p = .442). Because this re-analyzes Nosek and Smyth's (2011) original data to test the robustness of their reported finding, it is an actual empirical reproduction (`record_type: "reproduction"`). The only shipped row for this paper is row 1499 (Lane, Goh, & Driver-Linn, 2011/2012, 'Implicit Science Stereotypes Mediate the Relationship between Gender and Academic Participation', DOI `10.1007/s11199-011-0036-z`), which corresponds to sibling target 0 (replicated with a new sample of N = 514 in Part 2, pp. 14–15 and Appendix C) and is a completely distinct work from Nosek and Smyth (2011). Per review instructions when no paper outcome is requested, `outcome` is set to `cannot_be_determined`.

corrected_value.authors: Cornelissen K. K., McCarty K., Cornelissen P. L. & Tovée M. J.
corrected_value.title: Body size estimation in women with anorexia nervosa and healthy controls using 3D avatars

decisions.quote: In summary, the current study serves both as a replication and extension of Cornelissen et al. [17,18]. We aimed to replicate the differences in perceptual body image identified in these previous studies by improving the design in the following ways: a) ensuring a more accurate alignment of actual BMI ranges across participant groups, b) incorporating measures to control for sociocultural attitudes towards appearance, and c) implementing a refined psychophysical method for body size estimation that avoided emotionally loaded language in the responses.
decisions.reason: The primary source ( Irvine et al., 2024, DOI `10.1371/journal.pone.0313619`) explicitly states in the Introduction (lines 150–152) that 'the current study serves both as a replication and extension of Cornelissen et al. [17,18]' and aims 'to replicate the differences in perceptual body image identified in these previous studies' (the group-by-actual-BMI interaction in self-estimated BMI and the independent contribution of psychological factors in women with a history of anorexia nervosa vs. healthy controls), and directly compares its empirical results to both [17] and [18] throughout the Results (lines 382–385) and Discussion (lines 517–536, 561–593). References [17] and [18] are two separate empirical articles: [17] is Cornelissen et al. (2015, Body Image, 13, 75–85, DOI `10.1016/j.bodyim.2015.01.001`, testing women with current anorexia spectrum disorder using standard 2D CGI stimuli), and [18] is Cornelissen, McCarty, Cornelissen, & Tovée (2017, Scientific Reports, 7, 15773, DOI `10.1038/s41598-017-15339-z`, testing women with current or past eating-disorder history using 3D avatars). The single shipped row (row 1858, originally listing Reference [20], Cornelissen et al., 2016, DOI `10.1111/bjhp.12185`) was already adjudicated to represent blind target 0 (Reference [17], Cornelissen et al., 2015, `10.1016/j.bodyim.2015.01.001`), leaving Reference [18] (Cornelissen et al., 2017, `10.1038/s41598-017-15339-z`) as a genuinely distinct and unrepresented missing replication target. Per review instructions when no paper outcome is requested, `outcome` is set to `cannot_be_determined`.
